title: Bytes, pages and durability: a log-structured store
goal: By the end you can say when a write is really on disk, build a Bitcask-style store that appends every change to one file and indexes it in RAM, and recover that store after a crash tears its last record.

warmup.q: Your service calls `channel.write(buf)` on a `FileChannel`. The call returns, and one millisecond later the machine loses power. Is the record on disk?
options: Yes: `write` returned, so the bytes are in the file
Only if the JVM had flushed its own buffer for that channel
Not necessarily: `write` copied the bytes into the kernel's memory, and only `force()` waits for the drive
Yes, because an SSD has no moving parts and stores data instantly
warmup.why: `FileChannel.write` returns once the kernel holds a copy in its page cache, which is RAM. The kernel writes it to the drive later, often seconds later. `force()` (fsync) is the call that waits until the drive reports the data stored. The second option is the tempting one, but `FileChannel` has no JVM-side buffer: flushing a `BufferedOutputStream` only moves bytes into the kernel, not onto the drive.

sections.h: A write is not on disk until you force it
sections.body:
A payment service receives an authorization, `auth:9001` is `AUTHORIZED`, and must keep it through a crash. The simplest thing that could work is to append it to a file and reply OK:

```kotlin
channel.write(ByteBuffer.wrap("auth:9001=AUTHORIZED\n".encodeToByteArray()))
return Response.ok()
```

That `write` returns in about a microsecond, and it is not safe. When it returns, your bytes are not on the SSD. They are in the **page cache**: memory where the kernel keeps a copy of file data, in fixed-size blocks called pages (lesson 9 of the OS track, The page cache, writeback and fsync). The kernel copies changed pages to the drive later, usually within seconds. If the power fails first, the authorization is gone, and the caller was already told OK.

So version 2 asks the kernel to wait for the drive. In Java that is `FileChannel.force`. On Linux, `force(false)` calls `fdatasync` and `force(true)` calls `fsync`, the two system calls that wait for the drive (`fdatasync` skips file details such as the modification time when it can). Both return only when the drive reports the data stored. On macOS the JDK calls `fcntl(F_FULLFSYNC)`, which also makes the drive empty its own small write cache. A write is **durable** once force has returned: a power cut can no longer lose it.

Version 2 is correct and slow. The demo for this section appends 1,000 records of 100 bytes three ways. On an Apple Silicon MacBook it printed:

```text
write only              1,000 records in      7.0 ms  =    141,893 records/s
force every record      1,000 records in   4324.6 ms  =        231 records/s
force every 50          1,000 records in    102.2 ms  =      9,782 records/s
```

Each force waits about 4.3 ms, so one thread can make at most about 230 records a second durable, 600 times fewer than it can write. A payment API taking 2,000 authorizations a second can't wait 4 ms for each one in turn.

Version 3 keeps the rule and shares the cost. One force makes durable every byte written before it, so let several requests write, force once, then reply to all of them. Forcing once per 50 records needs 20 forces instead of 1,000 and gets about 10,000 records a second. This is **group commit**, and PostgreSQL does it too: one flush of its log (the next section introduces it) can make many transactions' commits durable at once.

Two physical facts sit under these numbers. The kernel and the drive never move single bytes; they move whole pages. `getconf PAGESIZE` prints 16384 on an Apple Silicon Mac and 4096 in the Linux container you'll use for PostgreSQL, and PostgreSQL reads and writes its tables in 8 KB pages. And appending is the cheapest write there is: every record goes at the end of one file, so the drive gets one sequential stream and never has to change data it already holds.

That gives the picture for the whole lesson, in the figure. The store is one file that only grows at the end, forced before every reply, plus a hash map in the JVM heap that remembers where each key's newest value sits in the file. The file is the truth. The map lives in RAM, so a crash wipes it, and the store must rebuild it from the file. The next three sections build each part.

One warning about force itself. In 2018 PostgreSQL developers found that Linux before 4.13 could lose a write-back error: it marked the failed pages clean, so a retried fsync returned success for data that never reached the drive. PostgreSQL now stops with a PANIC when an fsync fails and recovers from its log on restart. Do the same in your code: if `force` throws, don't retry and carry on.

try.title: Time write against force
steps: Predict: if one force takes about 4 ms, how long do 1,000 forced records take?
From `labs/`, run the demo with the command below.
Change `val batch = 50` to `10`, run it, then try `200`. Watch the third line.

Optional, PostgreSQL's own measurement inside Docker's Linux VM: start the database with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait`, then run `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec -u postgres db pg_test_fsync -s 2 -f /tmp/fsync.test`. Leave the database running for the next Try it.

code.title: FsyncDemo.kt

try.expect: On an Apple Silicon MacBook, write only takes a few milliseconds, force every record takes about 4.2 to 4.4 seconds (about 230 records a second), and force every 50 takes 100 to 160 ms. A batch of 10 lands in between and 200 is faster again: the cost follows the number of forces, not the number of bytes. Your numbers depend on the drive and the OS. `pg_test_fsync` reported about 12,000 to 13,000 `fdatasync` calls a second inside the VM here. That VM's virtual disk does not necessarily flush the Mac's drive cache, so don't read it as what the SSD can really do.

sections.h: Append every change and keep the index in RAM
sections.body:
The file keeps authorizations safe, but how do you read `auth:9001` back? The simplest answer is a scan: read the file from the start and keep the last value you see for that key. With a million records of about 40 bytes, every `get` reads 40 MB. Even from the page cache that is milliseconds per lookup, and it grows with every write.

The next idea is to update in place: give each key a fixed spot in the file and overwrite it. That breaks twice. Values have different lengths (`PENDING` is 7 bytes, `CAPTURED` is 8), so a fixed spot is either too small or wasteful. And a crash in the middle of an overwrite leaves a value that is half old and half new, with no copy of either.

**Bitcask**, the storage engine Basho built for the Riak database in 2010, keeps the append-only file and adds a hash map in memory. Every `put` appends a **record**: a 20-byte header, then the key, then the value. The figure shows the exact layout your lab uses. The in-memory map, called the **keydir**, maps each key to where its newest value starts in the file and how many bytes it has. So `get` is one hash lookup and one positional read, `channel.read(buffer, position)`, of exactly the value's bytes. A missing key costs no I/O at all. The Bitcask paper says a read never needs more than one disk seek (one trip to the drive), and that holds by construction.

An overwrite never touches the old record. `put("auth:9001", "CAPTURED")` appends a new record and moves the keydir entry to it, and the old `AUTHORIZED` record stays behind as dead bytes. A delete can't erase anything either, so it appends a **tombstone**: a record with the key and no value (value size -1). The keydir drops the key, and when the store later rebuilds the keydir from the file, the tombstone tells it the key is gone.

This design has two hard limits, and you should know them before you pick it. The keydir must hold every key in RAM: 50 million idempotency keys of 40 bytes, plus a map entry each, is several gigabytes of heap. And a hash map has no order, so "every capture for card 4242 between 9:00 and 10:00" means checking every key. B+trees (lesson 4) and LSM trees (lesson 5) exist to fix exactly that.

PostgreSQL uses the same append-first idea for durability. Before it changes a table page, it appends a record describing the change to its **write-ahead log** (WAL): an append-only file of change records. A commit is durable once the WAL has been forced past the commit's own record; the table pages are written later. Every position in the WAL is a byte offset called an **LSN** (log sequence number), and you can watch it move.

try.title: Watch PostgreSQL append to its log
steps: If PostgreSQL is not running yet, start it from `labs/` with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait`, then open psql with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz`.
Create the table and insert one row: `CREATE TABLE auth_log (id bigint, card text, status text);` then `INSERT INTO auth_log VALUES (1, 'card-4242', 'AUTHORIZED');`

Paste the block below. It notes the WAL position, inserts one row, notes the position again and runs `pg_waldump`, PostgreSQL's tool for printing WAL records, on exactly those bytes. (`\gset` saves a query result in a psql variable, `\setenv` copies it into the environment, and `\!` runs a shell command inside the container.)
Paste the block a second time. The first run can also show records PostgreSQL writes for its own catalog soon after start-up. Read the second run.

code.title: psql
code.src:
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn() AS before \gset
INSERT INTO auth_log VALUES (2, 'card-4242', 'CAPTURED');
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn() AS after \gset
SELECT :'before' AS before, :'after' AS after, pg_wal_lsn_diff(:'after', :'before') AS bytes;
\setenv B :before
\setenv E :after
\! pg_waldump -p /var/lib/postgresql/18/docker/pg_wal -s $B -e $E

try.expect:
The row costs 128 bytes of WAL. `pg_waldump` shows exactly two records:

```text
  before   |   after   | bytes
-----------+-----------+-------
 0/22AB178 | 0/22AB1F8 |   128

rmgr: Heap        len (rec/tot):     82/    82, tx:        867, lsn: 0/022AB178, ... desc: INSERT off: 3, ... blk 0
rmgr: Transaction len (rec/tot):     34/    34, tx:        867, lsn: 0/022AB1D0, ... desc: COMMIT 2026-11-07 17:54:44.732723 UTC
```

(output trimmed). An 82-byte INSERT record and a 34-byte COMMIT record, each padded to 8 bytes. Your LSNs and transaction ids differ. Run it again and the new `before` equals the old `after`: the log is one stream with no gaps, and it only moves forward.

sections.h: A crash tears the last record, and the CRC finds it
sections.body:
Now pull the plug. A crash can stop an append halfway, so the file may end with part of a record. That is a **torn write**. Every earlier record was forced before its `put` returned, so the damage can only be in the last record: the **torn tail**. On restart the keydir is empty, and the store rebuilds it by reading the file from offset 0, record by record. The hard part is knowing where the good records stop.

Version 1 trusts the header: read 20 bytes, take the key and value sizes, read that many bytes, repeat to the end of the file. It breaks at once. If the crash cut the last record after 13 bytes, there isn't even a whole header. Worse, a half-written header can hold any bytes at all, such as a key size of 2,147,483,647, and the scan would try to allocate a 2 GB buffer.

Version 2 checks the sizes. It stops if fewer than 20 bytes are left, if a size is negative, or if the record claims more bytes than the file has. That catches every record that is cut short. It still believes bytes that are present but wrong: a crash can leave zeros at the end of a file, and a damaged sector can flip a byte inside a value without touching the sizes.

Version 3 adds a checksum. When the store writes a record, it computes a **CRC-32C**, a 32-bit number calculated from every byte after the CRC field, and stores it in the record's first 4 bytes. Changing any single byte always changes the CRC, and random damage slips past it only about once in four billion tries. The scan recomputes it, so the full check for each record is:

1. If fewer than 20 bytes are left, the header is torn. Stop.
2. Read the header. If a size is impossible (negative, or longer than what is left of the file), stop.
3. Read the whole record and compute its CRC-32C. If it doesn't match the stored one, stop.
4. Otherwise apply it to the keydir (a tombstone removes the key) and move on.

Where the scan stops, the store **truncates** the file: it cuts it back to the end of the last good record. This step is easy to forget. Without it, the next append lands after the garbage, the next restart stops at the garbage again, and every record written in between disappears.

Throwing the torn record away loses nothing anyone was promised. Its `put` never returned, so no caller was told it succeeded. The client sees a timeout or an error and retries, and an idempotency key makes that retry harmless. This is the payoff of "force, then reply": a crash can lose a request the client knows has failed, never a write it was told had succeeded.

PostgreSQL ends crash recovery the same way. Every WAL record carries a CRC-32C. After a crash the server replays WAL records from its last checkpoint (a recent point by which all earlier changes had reached the table files) until a record fails its checks, and that failure is how it finds the end of the log. The stepper walks through the lab's version, and the Try it makes PostgreSQL do it for real.

stepper.title: Append, crash, recover
stepper.intro: Four puts, a power cut in the middle of the fourth, and a restart. Use Next and Back, or the arrow keys.

try.title: Pull the plug on PostgreSQL
steps: From `labs/`, with PostgreSQL still running from the previous Try it, add 1,000 rows and note the count: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -c "INSERT INTO auth_log SELECT g, 'card-' || g, 'AUTHORIZED' FROM generate_series(3, 1002) g;" -c "SELECT count(*) FROM auth_log;"`
Kill the server the way a power cut would, with no chance to shut down cleanly, then start it again (the commands below).

When you are done with this lesson, stop and delete the database with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml down -v`.

code.title: terminal, in labs/

docker compose -f env/postgres.yml kill -s SIGKILL db
docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait
docker compose -f env/postgres.yml logs db | grep -E 'not properly|redo (starts|done)|invalid'

try.expect:
The log shows a crash recovery that ends at the first bad record:

```text
LOG:  database system was not properly shut down; automatic recovery in progress
LOG:  redo starts at 0/21DFD80
LOG:  invalid record length at 0/221EE20: expected at least 24, got 0
LOG:  redo done at 0/221EDF8 ...
```

(timestamps trimmed). The `invalid record` line is not an error: it is the scan reaching bytes that are not a whole record, exactly like the lab's torn tail. On another run it said `invalid magic number 0000 in WAL segment ...` because the log ended at a page boundary. The count is the same as before the kill, because every committed row was in the WAL before its COMMIT returned.

sections.h: Overwrites pile up until you merge
sections.body:
The store survives crashes now, but its file never shrinks. Every overwrite and every tombstone adds bytes, and dead records stay forever. In the lab's merge test, ten card balances updated 100 times each leave 1,000 records: about 36 KB of file for 370 bytes of live data. File size divided by live data is the **space amplification**, here about 100.

The obvious fix is to tidy the file in place, sliding live records down over dead ones. A crash halfway through would destroy records that haven't been moved yet, so that's out.

The safe fix is a **merge** (other systems call it compaction). Read the keydir, write one record per live key into a new file, force the new file, then rename it over the old one. A rename within one file system is atomic: after a crash you find either the old file or the new one, never half of each. Swap in a keydir with the new offsets, and the dead records are gone, tombstones included.

Real Bitcask merges without stopping writers. It closes the active file once it reaches a size limit and starts a new one, so older files never change again, and a background merge reads only those closed files. Next to each merged file it writes a **hint file**: just keys and positions, no values. On restart, reading the hint files rebuilds the keydir without reading every value. Your lab keeps one file and merges it whole, which is enough to see the mechanism. With one file a tombstone can be dropped at once. With many files it must stay until every older file holding that key has been merged, or the old value would come back.

Merging costs writes. A live value is written once by its `put` and again by every merge that copies it. Bytes written to disk divided by bytes the application asked to write is the **write amplification**. Every log-structured design trades it against space: merge often and the file stays small but the drive writes more; merge rarely and the reverse. RocksDB's documentation says its default leveled compaction often has write amplification above 10, and lesson 5 of this track measures it in an LSM tree.

analogy: Think of a bound ledger written in pen. You never erase a line: a correction is a new line at the bottom, and a slip of paper at the front lists, for each account, the line that holds its latest balance. Every line ends with a check digit, so if the pen ran dry halfway through the last line you can see it and ignore it. When the book fills up, you copy just the latest line per account into a new book and throw the old one away. The analogy breaks at the slip of paper: in Bitcask the index lives only in RAM, so after a crash nobody has it, and you rebuild it by reading the whole book from the first line.
in_your_world: You already run this design. A Kafka partition is an append-only log split into segment files, and the broker leans on the OS page cache: it gets durability from replication, where `acks=all` counts a record as written once every in-sync replica has it, not from an fsync per message. Oracle's redo log is a write-ahead log: at COMMIT the log writer process (LGWR) writes your redo to disk, and the data files catch up later. In your own services, the rule of this lesson applies to every "save, then acknowledge" path. The authorization API must not return 200 before the database COMMIT returns, a Kafka consumer must not commit its offset before the ledger write is durable, and when a crash makes a client retry, the idempotency key is what turns the retry into a no-op.
mistake: The common mistake is acknowledging before the data is durable: writing with `FileChannel.write` or `Files.write`, or even committing to a database with `synchronous_commit = off`, and replying OK in the same breath. Tests never catch it, because tests don't pull the power. People make it because `write` returns success and the data is visible to every reader at once, so it looks stored. The fix is to put the force (or the synchronous commit) before the reply, and to make it cheap with group commit if throughput suffers, not to skip it.

compare.title: Acknowledging too early vs after force

a.label: Too early
a.title: loses acknowledged writes

b.label: After force
b.title: durable before the reply

compare.note: The two functions differ by one line and by about 4 ms on a MacBook. The first one passes every test you will write and loses captures you already confirmed when a machine dies. If the 4 ms hurts, batch: let several requests write, force once, then reply to all of them.

worked.title: Walk a recovery scan over a torn file

steps.say: After a crash, `data.log` is 113 bytes long. The keydir is empty. Start the scan at offset 0 and keep two numbers: `pos`, where the next record should start, and `size`, the file length.
steps.code:
size = 113, pos = 0
record length = 20 (header) + ksz + max(vsz, 0)

steps.say: Check the header at 0. At least 20 bytes are left, so read it: `ksz = 6`, `vsz = 7`, so the record is 33 bytes and fits. Read all 33 bytes, compute the CRC-32C over bytes 4 to 32 and compare it with the first 4 bytes. It matches, so apply it and move on.

Repeat at 33 (`auth:2`, 33 bytes) and at 66 (`auth:1` again, 34 bytes). The second `auth:1` record replaces the first in the keydir, because the scan applies records in file order and the later one is newer.
steps.code:
pos = 0    auth:1 -> value at 26, 7 bytes
pos = 33   auth:2 -> value at 59, 7 bytes
pos = 66   auth:1 -> value at 92, 8 bytes   (replaces the entry above)
pos = 100

steps.say: At 100, only 13 bytes are left. Check 1 fails, so the scan stops. Truncate the file to 100 and set `end = 100`. If instead all 34 bytes had been present but one value byte had flipped, checks 1 and 2 would pass and check 3 would stop the scan at the same place.

lab.title: Build a log-structured store that survives a torn tail
steps: Read `LogFormat.kt`. It is complete: `Record.encode` builds a record, `Record.crc` computes a CRC-32C, and the `*_AT` constants say where each header field sits.
Run the tests once. All 12 fail, because `open` calls `recover`, which is still a `TODO`.

Write `put`: append `Record.encode(key, value)` at `end` with the `writeFully` helper, call `channel.force(false)`, then point the keydir at the value (`end + HEADER_SIZE + key bytes`) and move `end` on. Write `delete` the same way with a tombstone.
Write `get`: one keydir lookup, one `readFully` of `valueSize` bytes at `valuePos`.
Write `recover` with the three checks from the worked example, then truncate at the first bad record. The torn-tail test cuts the last record at every possible byte, so every check gets exercised.
Write `merge`. Run the tests until all 12 pass.
hints: The test channel counts calls. If "get does exactly one read" fails, you are probably reading the header before the value. The keydir already knows the value's offset and length.
If "put and delete force the file" fails, the last thing `put` does to the channel must be `force`. Update the keydir after the force, not before.
Read header fields with absolute gets, such as `header.getInt(Record.KEY_SIZE_AT)`, so the buffer position doesn't matter.
In `merge`, read each live value from the old channel before you close it. Then `Files.move(tmp, path, ATOMIC_MOVE, REPLACE_EXISTING)` and reopen with `channels.open(path)`.

drill.title: Write a durable append from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. In a blank file, write `fun append(ch: FileChannel, rec: ByteBuffer, at: Long): Long`. It writes the whole record at offset `at`, makes it durable, and returns the offset where the next record goes. Then write, as comments, the three checks recovery makes on each record before it trusts it.

recap: `write` puts bytes in the kernel's page cache. Only `force` (fsync, or `F_FULLFSYNC` on macOS) waits for the drive, so reply OK only after it returns.
A force costs milliseconds on a laptop. Append to one file and batch forces (group commit) to make durability affordable.
Bitcask appends every put and delete to one file and keeps a keydir in RAM, so a get is one hash lookup and one positional read.
A crash can only tear the last record. Recovery scans from the start, checks sizes and the CRC, stops at the first bad record and truncates there.
Overwrites and tombstones pile up. A merge rewrites the live records into a new file and renames it into place, trading write amplification for space.
The keydir must hold every key in RAM and has no order, so range queries need a B+tree or an LSM tree.

quiz.q: To save latency, an authorization service appends each request to a log with `write`, replies OK at once, and a background thread calls `force` every 100 ms. What happens if the machine loses power?
options: Nothing is lost, because the background thread forces the file soon after
Up to about 100 ms of authorizations that were already confirmed to clients can disappear
Only the request being written at that moment can be lost
The log becomes unreadable, so every authorization is lost
quiz.why: Every record written since the last force may still be only in the page cache, and the service already said OK for all of them. The third option describes the safe design, where the reply waits for the force. The log is not unreadable: recovery keeps everything up to the torn tail.

quiz.q: You plan a Bitcask-style store for 200 million idempotency keys of about 40 bytes each, with values of 300 bytes. What runs out first?
options: Disk space, because the values are large
RAM, because the keydir holds every key and its position in memory
CPU, because every get computes a CRC
File handles, because each key needs its own file
quiz.why: 200 million keys at 40 bytes is 8 GB before any map overhead, and the keydir must hold all of them in RAM. The values, 60 GB, sit on disk, which is cheap. Reads don't need to verify the CRC on every get, and Bitcask uses a few large files, not one per key.

quiz.q: On restart, the scan finds that the last record in the file has the right sizes but a CRC that does not match. What should recovery do?
options: Keep the record, since the sizes prove it was completely written
Repair the bytes using the CRC, then apply the record
Skip that record and keep scanning for more records after it
Stop there and truncate the file at the start of that record
quiz.why: A CRC mismatch means the bytes are not what was written, so the record cannot be trusted, and its put never returned, so dropping it loses nothing that was promised. A CRC detects damage but cannot repair it. Skipping ahead is a trap: the sizes of a damaged record can't be trusted to say where the next record starts.

quiz.q: One `force` takes 4 ms on your drive, and one thread writes the log. Roughly how many durable commits per second can it do with a force per commit, and with one force per batch of 20 commits?
options: About 250, and about 5,000
About 250 in both cases, because the drive is the limit
About 4,000, and about 80,000
About 5,000 in both cases, because appends are sequential
quiz.why: 1 second / 4 ms = 250 forces a second. If each force covers 20 commits, the same 250 forces make 5,000 commits durable. The drive limits forces, not commits, which is why group commit works. Each commit in a batch waits a little longer, up to one batch window.

quiz.q: A product manager wants "all captures for card 4242 between 09:00 and 10:00" from the Bitcask store, where keys look like `card:4242:2026-11-07T09:15:03`. What does the store have to do?
options: One positional read, because the keydir knows where every key is
Scan every key in the keydir, because a hash table keeps no order
Read only the newest part of the file, because the log is in time order
Use the hint file, which stores keys in sorted order
quiz.why: A hash table answers "where is exactly this key" and nothing else, so a range means checking every key. The log is in write order, but writes for one card are mixed with every other card's, and old values may be dead. Hint files list keys and positions, not sorted ranges. Ordered indexes (B+trees, LSM trees) come later in this track for this reason.

flashcards.front: When `FileChannel.write` returns, where are your bytes?
flashcards.back: In the kernel's page cache, in RAM. They reach the drive later, unless you call `force`.

flashcards.front: What does `FileChannel.force(false)` call on Linux, and on macOS?
flashcards.back: `fdatasync` on Linux. On macOS the JDK calls `fcntl(F_FULLFSYNC)`, which also flushes the drive's own write cache.
An in-memory hash table from each live key to the position and size of its newest value in the data file. A get is one lookup plus one positional read.

flashcards.front: What is a torn tail, and how does recovery spot it?
flashcards.back: A last record that was only partly written when the system crashed. Recovery spots it because too few bytes are left, the sizes don't fit the file, or the CRC doesn't match.

flashcards.front: What goes wrong if recovery does not truncate the torn tail?
flashcards.back: The next append lands after the garbage. The next restart stops at the garbage and drops every record written since.
Making many writes durable with one force. Each force covers every byte written before it, so commits that arrive together share the cost of one fsync.
It saves space by rewriting only live records into a new file, and pays for it in write amplification: the same values get written to disk again.

terms.plain: The kernel's in-memory copy of file data. Writes land here first.
The call that waits until the drive reports your written data is stored.
A file that is only ever written at the end. Old records are never changed.
Bitcask's in-memory hash table from key to the position of its newest value.
A record that marks a key as deleted, because an append-only file cannot erase.
A write cut short by a crash, leaving part of a record on disk.
A 32-bit checksum stored with each record so a reader can tell whether the bytes are intact.
How many bytes reach the disk for each byte the application wrote, counting rewrites by merges.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate says: "Our event store appends to a file and the write call returns success, so after a crash we can't lose an event we've acknowledged." Explain what can still go wrong, and what the store must do on write and on restart.
explain_back.answer: A successful write only means the kernel has the bytes in its page cache. If the machine loses power before the kernel writes them out, acknowledged events disappear. So the store must call force (fsync) before it acknowledges, and can batch several events per force to keep the cost down. A crash can also leave the last record half written. On restart the store has to scan the file from the start, check each record's sizes and CRC, stop at the first record that fails, and truncate the file there. Dropping that record is safe because it was never acknowledged, and the truncate stops new appends from landing behind garbage that a later restart would trip over.

deeper.body:
Three details that matter once this runs in production.

**The directory needs an fsync too.** A merge creates a file and renames it. The new file's contents are durable after you force the file, but the rename lives in the directory, which is a separate file. On Linux you open the directory itself and fsync it, or a crash right after the rename can bring back the old name. The JDK lets you open a directory as a read-only `FileChannel` and force it on Linux and macOS. It is not portable to every OS, which is one reason the lab skips it.

**Corruption in the middle is a different failure.** The lab stops at the first bad record wherever it is. At the tail that is right. A bad record in the middle of a forced file means the drive or file system damaged data after the fact, and stopping there throws away good records behind it. Real systems react differently: PostgreSQL ends WAL replay at the first invalid record, while data page checksums (on by default for new clusters since PostgreSQL 18) report damaged table pages with an error instead of silently dropping them. Bitcask's merge and hint files also carry CRCs so damage is detected, not repaired.

**Torn pages, not just torn records.** A database that overwrites 8 KB pages in place can have a page that is half old and half new after a crash, because drives write in 512-byte or 4 KB units. PostgreSQL guards against this by writing a full image of each page into the WAL the first time the page changes after a checkpoint (`full_page_writes`), and InnoDB writes pages twice through its doublewrite buffer. An append-only store sidesteps the problem: it never overwrites a page that holds live data. Lesson 6 of this track comes back to torn pages when you build a write-ahead log.
